questions.question: Traffic between VLANs 10 and 20 is routed at wire speed inside the same chassis that switches the frames - no external router is involved. What type of switch performs both roles?
questions.explanation: A switch that also routes between VLANs (inter-VLAN routing) using dedicated hardware is a multilayer or Layer 3 switch; a pure Layer 2 switch would need an external router to cross VLAN boundaries.

questions.question: Two parallel uplinks between switches create a broadcast storm until a protocol elects a root bridge and blocks the redundant path while keeping it in reserve. Which protocol breaks the loop?
questions.explanation: Redundant Layer 2 paths form loops that broadcast storms exploit; STP builds a loop-free tree to a root bridge and deliberately places redundant links in the blocking state.

questions.question: A latency-critical trading desk picks a switch that begins forwarding a frame after reading only the destination MAC - it never waits for or checks the FCS. Which switching method is it using?
questions.explanation: Forwarding after the destination address (~14 bytes) minimizes latency but can propagate corrupt frames - that is cut-through; store-and-forward would buffer the whole frame and check the FCS first.

questions.question: A switch buffers every frame in full, verifies its CRC, and discards corrupted frames before forwarding - trading higher latency for error checking. Which switching method is this?
questions.explanation: Receiving the entire frame lets the switch validate the FCS/CRC and filter errors before transmission; that full-buffering behavior defines store-and-forward, the opposite of cut-through.

questions.question: Frames for VLANs 10, 20, and 30 must cross a single physical link between two switches, each frame carrying an 802.1Q tag. How must the ports on that link be configured?
questions.explanation: An access port carries exactly one untagged VLAN; carrying tagged frames for several VLANs over one link requires configuring the ports as trunks (802.1Q trunking).

questions.question: A core router advertises 10.1.0.0/24, 10.1.1.0/24, 10.1.2.0/24, and 10.1.3.0/24 as one 10.1.0.0/22 entry to shrink the upstream routing table. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: The four contiguous /24s share their top 22 bits, so a single /22 covers them exactly. Advertising one shorter prefix in place of many specific ones is route summarization (aggregation/supernetting).

questions.question: A firewall permits return traffic for sessions initiated from inside with no inbound rules at all, because it tracks each connection's state in a table. Which firewall type is this?
questions.explanation: A stateless filter would need explicit rules for return traffic; recognizing replies as part of an existing connection - by tracking a state table - is stateful inspection.

questions.question: A small office replaces its separate modem, router, four-port switch, and Wi-Fi access point with one ISP-supplied box that performs all four roles. What kind of device is it?
questions.explanation: Consumer gateways combine routing, switching, wireless access, and often modem functions in a single appliance - commonly called an integrated or wireless router.

questions.question: VoWiFi phones drop calls when nurses walk between access points because re-authentication takes too long; the fix pre-authenticates clients to neighboring APs before the roam. Which 802.11 amendment provides this fast transition?
questions.explanation: 802.11r (Fast BSS Transition) lets a client pre-establish security state with target APs so the roaming handoff completes in tens of milliseconds instead of re-running full authentication.

questions.question: A switch sustains line-rate forwarding on all 48 ports simultaneously because forwarding decisions run in dedicated silicon rather than on the CPU. Which component makes this possible?
questions.explanation: General-purpose CPUs cannot forward 48 gigabit flows at once; ASICs are chips hard-wired for the switching lookup pipeline, delivering wire-speed forwarding per port.

questions.question: A compromise between cut-through and store-and-forward waits only until the first 64 bytes - the collision window - of a frame arrive before forwarding it. Which switching method is this?
questions.explanation: Most collision damage appears in the first 64 bytes (the minimum legal frame/collision window); reading just that far before forwarding is fragment-free, also called modified cut-through.

questions.question: A legacy LAN still runs the original spanning tree, which spends roughly 30-50 seconds in listening and learning states before a port forwards. Which IEEE standard defines it?
questions.explanation: Classic STP with its blocking-listening-learning-forwarding progression and slow convergence is IEEE 802.1D; the faster 802.1w variant is RSTP.

questions.question: Two Cisco routers present one virtual default-gateway IP and MAC to hosts; if the active router fails, the standby silently takes over the virtual identity. Which Cisco-proprietary FHRP is this?
questions.explanation: Cisco's proprietary first-hop redundancy protocol elects an active and standby router that share a virtual IP/MAC for gateway failover - VRRP is the open-standard counterpart.

questions.question: After a topology change the LAN reconverges in about six seconds using proposal/agreement synchronization defined by IEEE 802.1w. Which spanning-tree variant is running?
questions.explanation: 802.1w Rapid STP replaces 802.1D's timer-driven states with a handshake-based proposal/agreement mechanism, cutting convergence from 30-50 seconds to a few seconds.

questions.question: An audit finds access ports automatically becoming trunks because they still negotiate link mode with a neighboring Cisco switch - a known VLAN-hopping risk. Which proprietary protocol should be disabled?
questions.explanation: Dynamic Trunking Protocol negotiates trunk formation between Cisco ports; left enabled it can let an attacker form an unauthorized trunk and hop VLANs, so hardened configs set ports manually and disable DTP.

questions.question: A fully populated switch replaces a hub on a busy Ethernet segment; every one of its two dozen ports has a host attached. How many separate collision domains result?
questions.explanation: Each switch port is its own collision domain, so all 24 populated ports create 24 collision domains; the hub it replaced had only one.

questions.question: Frames arrive at a switch destined for a MAC address that is not yet in its address table. What does the switch do with those frames?
questions.answer: floods them out all ports except the incoming port
questions.explanation: A switch floods frames with an unknown destination MAC out every port except the one they arrived on until it learns the address.

questions.question: An attacker floods a switch with frames from spoofed source addresses until it starts forwarding traffic out of every port. Which switch table was exhausted?
questions.explanation: A CAM table overflow attack fills the switch's MAC address table so it floods frames to all ports like a hub.

questions.question: A router connects three separate LAN segments, one per routed interface. How many broadcast domains exist across this topology?
questions.explanation: Routers do not forward broadcasts, so each routed interface delimits a separate broadcast domain - 3 interfaces means 3 domains.

questions.question: A router receives a packet whose destination matches no route entry and no default route is configured. What does the router do with the packet?
alternatives: drops the packet (and sends an ICMP destination unreachable message)
questions.explanation: With no matching route and no default gateway of last resort, the router drops the packet and typically returns an ICMP destination unreachable message.
